task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-05-23, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
If PNR fail then PULL_UP is a real league-wide counter, it should show lift>0 in >=70% of units with median lift>2pp.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: How to define PNR failure from play-by-play data?
How to define and isolate PULL_UP counter possessions after PNR failure?
What unit of analysis (team, team-season, matchup) is appropriate for testing lift across units?
How to measure lift (baseline, adjustment) and estimate sampling variability?
What sample size is needed to reliably detect median lift >0.02 with 70% positive units?
How to control for regression-to-the-mean when selecting on H1-to-H2 decline?
How to separate counter effectiveness from opponent defensive quality changes?

historical_evidence.finding: PNR shot-level season rates vs possession labels: 2024-25 shot-level PNR share of half-court shots ranges from OKC 7.567% to IND 13.824%. Descriptive calibration input for PBPProxyPNR.
TOV_FORCE 3-ply adversarial surviving lift: R1 lifts shrink ~50%+ after opponent re-route and follow-the-ball counter. Many cells used n<10 surrogates. Net lift is model-implied, not observed.
Relative-structure single-game validation BOS vs OKC: one game, 5-6 play types per team with 4-35 possessions. Inconclusive; question not answerable with the design.
Adversarial best-response v1: equilibrium strategy vs actual +1.16 pts/100; beats actual 53% of matchups. Doc verdict MARGINAL; equilibrium PPP is model-implied not observed.

failed_approaches.what_failed: single-game validation of play-type rank ordering
failed_approaches.why: untestable due to one game with very small possessions per play type (4-35), yielding no statistical power (failure type A_unanswerable).

failed_approaches.what_failed: adversarial surviving lift estimation on turnover-force counter
failed_approaches.why: net lift is model-implied, not observed; many cells used additive surrogates at n<10; 4 games / 8 sides extreme sparsity.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Nash equilibrium counterfactual vs actual strategy
failed_approaches.why: inconclusive; marginal advantage; equilibrium PPP is model-implied, not directly observed. Not a hypothesis test of a specific counter.

evidence_establishes: Play-type classification for PNR from play-by-play data is operational (shot-level rates computed in [prior work]).
Counter-play lift estimates tend to shrink substantially when opponent adaptation is taken into account ([prior work]).
Very small sample sizes (single game, few possessions per play type) make counter-play lift untestable ([prior work]).
Model-implied PPP can differ from observed outcomes and may yield inconclusive results ([prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether PULL_UP is an effective counter after PNR suppression/failure.
Any reliable estimate of the magnitude or sign of PULL_UP lift in such situations.
The typical number of 'units' (teams, team-seasons) that experience PNR failure triggers in this dataset.
That the study's play-type classifier for PULL_UP is sufficiently accurate for lift measurement.
That a league-wide test of the specific condition (>=70% units, median lift >2pp) is feasible with the available data.
own_inferences: The proposed unit is likely a team-season, giving at most 120 units over the four complete regular seasons.
PNR failure would typically be defined by a half-over-half decline in PNR PPP, creating a strong regression-to-the-mean bias in the selected trigger sample.
The counter lift would be measured by comparing PULL_UP PPP in trigger-game second halves to some baseline; this invites confounding by opponent defensive strength and game context.
PULL_UP possessions are less frequent than spot-up or drive, so per-unit sample sizes will often be below what is needed to reliably detect a 0.02 PPP lift.
The threshold of 'median lift > 2 percentage points' is a very small effect size relative to the typical standard error of per-unit PPP differences, requiring large samples per unit.
The combination of RTM selection and small sample is likely to produce an artifactual positive lift in many units, inflating the '70% positive' condition.
uncertainties: The precise operational definition of 'PNR fail' (e.g., half-level suppression trigger vs per-possession failure) is not specified.
The time window for the counter (immediate next possession, remainder of game, future games) is ambiguous.
The baseline for measuring lift (team's own season-average PULL_UP PPP, opponent-adjusted, or league average) is not defined.
The play-type classifier's accuracy for PULL_UP, especially in transition from PNR, is unknown from the available data catalog.
The number of games per season in which a team experiences a PNR suppression trigger is unknown and could be very small.
Whether the 2025-26 partial data are sufficient to use as full season is unclear.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records do not contain a previous decision on this specific research question. However, they inform the risk assessment by demonstrating that small-sample counter-lift studies are untestable ([prior work]) and that adversarial lift shrinks with adaptation ([prior work]), reinforcing concerns about power and confounding for the current question.

blocking_constraints.text: Per-unit trigger counts and PULL_UP possessions are likely too small for reliable detection of a 0.02 PPP lift; the condition '>=70% of units' and median lift test will be underpowered.
Defining PNR failure by a half-over-half PPP drop selects units with extreme H1 PPP, causing regression to the mean in subsequent PULL_UP performance and spurious positive lift.
Opponent defensive quality, game script, and lineup changes can simultaneously suppress PNR and affect PULL_UP efficiency, creating a correlation not causal counter effectiveness.
PULL_UP is not the most frequent play type; many trigger games will yield only a handful of PULL_UP possessions, making per-unit lift estimates highly unstable.
The trigger label (PNR fail) is derived from the same performance metric (PPP) used to evaluate lift, risking circularity and overfitting to noise.

prior_work.summary: No earlier study directly tested the PNR-failure -> PULL_UP counter lift hypothesis. Related work established PNR shot-level rates ([prior work]), explored adversarial counter lift shrinkage ([prior work]), and demonstrated that single-game or very-small-sample counter designs are untestable ([prior work]) or inconclusive ([prior work]).

risks.text: Expected number of team-seasons with enough trigger games and PULL_UP possessions to estimate lift will be small; power to test median lift > 0.02 across units is likely below conventional thresholds.
PULL_UP is a moderate-frequency play type; per-unit observations in trigger-game second halves may often fall below 20, making PPP difference estimates unreliable.
Team-games entering the trigger set due to low H2 PNR PPP will see their PULL_UP PPP regress upward even if no counter is effective, creating a positive bias in lift.
Defensive quality, strategic adjustments, and player availability are correlated with both PNR suppression and PULL_UP outcomes; simple baseline comparisons cannot fully remove this bias.
Using PPP drops to define triggers and then using PPP of another play type as outcome may capitalise on the same noise sources, inflating apparent effects.
The definition of 'PNR fail' and the identification of PULL_UP possessions rely on the accuracy of the rule-based classifier, which has not been validated for this specific counter setting.

If the analysis is extended to test multiple counter play types beyond PULL_UP, multiplicity adjustments will be needed; the current single-type test does not trigger this, but exploratory leakage is a risk.

design.estimand: Per-team-season mean difference in points per possession (PPP) on PULL_UP plays in games where the team's PNR was suppressed (trigger) versus the same team's average PULL_UP PPP in non-trigger games, after adjusting for opponent defensive rating. The league-wide test is whether at least 70% of team-seasons have positive lift and the median lift exceeds 0.02 PPP.
design.unit: team-season (e.g., BOS 2023, BOS 2024, ..., up to 120 units from four full regular seasons).
design.sample: All complete regular-season games from 2022-23 through 2025-26, excluding garbage time (period 4 with score margin > 15). Use only team-seasons with at least 5 trigger games and at least 30 observed PULL_UP possessions in trigger-game second halves.
design.power: Simulate power with realistic shot-level variance (std. dev. ~1.3 pts per possession). Even with 30 PULL_UP possessions per unit, the standard error of a mean difference is ~0.24 PPP. To detect a true 0.02 PPP lift with 80% power would require >100 possessions per unit, which is implausible for most teams. The median-of-units test is even less powerful. Estimated power <0.2.
design.controls: For each PULL_UP possession, record opponent season-long defensive rating, home/away, period, score margin, and starter indicator. Use a mixed-effects model with team-season random intercepts to estimate lift per unit, including these covariates.
design.falsification: Construct a placebo trigger by reversing the H1/H2 label within games: compute 'false trigger' where H1 PNR PPP is low relative to H2. If the RTM mechanism is responsible, we expect similar 'lift' for PULL_UP in placebo-trigger games. Additionally, shuffle team labels to break the association.
design.multiplicity: Single pre-registered test of the PULL_UP counter. No other play types or variations are tested.
design.decision_rule: Compute the per-unit adjusted lift estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Support requires: (i) the non-parametric bootstrap percentile confidence interval for the median lift excludes values ≤0.02, (ii) the point estimate of the proportion of units with lift > 0 exceeds 0.70 and the lower bound of its 95% binomial confidence interval exceeds 0.50.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular season play-by-play, with possession-level initiation records (Neo4j graph) frozen as of 2026-05-23. Exclude 2025-26 partial data beyond regular season.
